name: Glycine
note: The smallest amino acid, and the only achiral one — its alpha carbon carries two hydrogens. Its tiny side chain gives backbones unusual flexibility.
groupWhat: There is no side chain at all — only an H, which is why glycine is the smallest and the only achiral one.

name: Alanine
note: A simple methyl group — the reference point for a small hydrophobic side chain.
groupWhat: One carbon with its hydrogens. The simplest possible side chain, and completely unreactive.

name: Valine
note: Branched at the beta carbon. Branched hydrophobics cluster in protein cores.
groupWhat: Three carbons branching at the first one. Pure hydrocarbon, so it hides from water.

name: Leucine
note: Branched and strongly hydrophobic; very common in membrane-spanning helices.
groupWhat: Four carbons with a branch near the end. Pure hydrocarbon and strongly water-avoiding.

name: Isoleucine
note: One of two amino acids with a second stereocenter in the side chain (threonine is the other).
groupWhat: Four carbons branched at the first. Like valine and leucine, hydrocarbon only.

name: Methionine
note: Contains sulfur as a thioether. Always the first amino acid of a new protein — AUG is the start codon.
groupWhat: A sulfur sitting BETWEEN two carbons. Unlike a thiol it has no S–H, so it cannot form disulfides.

name: Proline
note: Its side chain loops back to the backbone nitrogen, making it a secondary amine. That ring locks rotation, so proline kinks helices and breaks sheets.
groupName: a ring back to the backbone
groupWhat: The side chain loops around and bonds to the backbone nitrogen, locking the geometry rigid.

name: Phenylalanine
note: Aromatic and hydrophobic — a plain benzene ring with no polar group on it.
groupWhat: A flat six-carbon aromatic ring with nothing polar on it, so it behaves as pure grease.

name: Tryptophan
note: The largest amino acid. Its indole ring dominates a protein's UV absorbance at 280 nm, which is how protein concentration is measured.
groupWhat: Two fused aromatic rings — the largest side chain of the twenty.

name: Serine
note: A small hydroxyl. Serine is a common active-site nucleophile and a frequent phosphorylation site.
groupWhat: An oxygen carrying a hydrogen: the same group that makes something an alcohol. It hydrogen bonds, and enzymes often use it as a nucleophile.

name: Threonine
note: A hydroxyl on a secondary carbon; like isoleucine it has a second stereocenter. Also phosphorylated.
groupWhat: The same alcohol group as serine, but on a carbon that also carries a methyl.

name: Cysteine
note: Two cysteines oxidize to form a disulfide bridge — the only covalent crosslink in tertiary structure. Its thiol pKa of ~8.3 is low enough to be partly deprotonated and highly nucleophilic.
groupWhat: A sulfur carrying a hydrogen — sulfur sits directly below oxygen, so a thiol is the sulfur version of an alcohol. More acidic and far more reactive, and two of them join into a disulfide bridge.

name: Tyrosine
note: Aromatic AND polar, because of the ring hydroxyl. Also a phosphorylation site, and contributes to absorbance at 280 nm.
groupWhat: A benzene ring carrying an –OH. Aromatic AND polar, because of that hydroxyl.

name: Asparagine
note: The amide of aspartate. Amides are neutral — do not confuse it with the acidic form. Common N-linked glycosylation site.
groupWhat: A C=O bonded to a nitrogen. Amides are NEUTRAL — this is the amide version of aspartate, not an acid.

name: Glutamine
note: The amide of glutamate, and likewise neutral.
groupWhat: The same neutral amide as asparagine, one carbon further out. The amide version of glutamate.

name: Aspartate
note: Carboxylate side chain, pKa ~3.9 — well below physiological pH, so it is deprotonated and negative in the body.
groupWhat: A carboxyl (–COOH) that has lost its proton. That is what makes it acidic and negatively charged in the body.

name: Glutamate
note: One carbon longer than aspartate, otherwise the same story: negative at physiological pH.
groupWhat: The same acidic group as aspartate, one carbon further from the backbone.

name: Lysine
note: A long flexible chain ending in a primary amine, pKa ~10.5 — protonated and positive at physiological pH.
groupWhat: A long flexible chain ending in a nitrogen. Nitrogen grabs a proton, so it carries a positive charge at body pH.

name: Arginine
note: The most basic side chain, pKa ~12.5. Its guanidinium group is resonance-stabilized, so it stays positive under essentially all physiological conditions.
groupWhat: A nitrogen-rich group whose positive charge is spread over three nitrogens by resonance, so it stays charged under essentially all conditions.

name: Histidine
note: The one to know cold: pKa ~6.0 sits near physiological pH, so histidine can gain or lose a proton under normal conditions. That makes it the workhorse of enzyme active sites and the only side chain that buffers well at pH 7.
groupWhat: A five-membered ring containing two nitrogens. Its pKa of 6.0 sits near body pH, so it can pick up or hand off a proton — which is why it does the chemistry in so many enzymes.
